name: Lemon juice lightening

lead: Lemon juice lightening is a folk practice in which people apply lemon juice to skin to brighten dark spots or marks, or to hair with sun exposure for natural highlights. The appeal is that lemons are cheap and contain citric acid.
Wikipedia notes lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid and is sometimes used to lighten hair after sun exposure, citing a magazine and a hair-care brand.

paras: People dab or spray juice on spots or hair, then sometimes sit in sunlight for hair highlights. Skin versions are often diluted or mixed with other pantry items.

Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction after contact with plant furanocoumarins, such as in lime juice, followed by UVA exposure; it can cause redness and blisters, and leave dark marks lasting years. Lime is the best-known culprit; the source does not name lemon specifically.

angle.text: People use the juice hoping for a brighter complexion or natural hair highlights, using a pantry ingredient.

lead: Lemon juice lightening is a do-it-yourself practice of applying lemon juice to skin or hair to lighten. Users want brighter-looking spots or sun-lightened hair highlights. [1]
Wikipedia reports lemon juice is roughly 5 to 6 percent citric acid and that it is sometimes used on moistened hair, which is then exposed to sunlight, as a natural highlight. [1]

Dermatology references describe phytophotodermatitis, a phototoxic skin reaction after contact with light-sensitizing plant substances such as lime juice followed by UVA. Reactions start within 24 hours, peak at 48 to 72 hours, may blister, and can leave dark marks that last several years. [2]
infobox: Phototoxic reactions with citrus and UVA

paras: Lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid. [1] It is used on hair with sun exposure for highlights. [1]

Phytophotodermatitis is triggered by furanocoumarins plus UVA (320-380 nm); the reaction is non-immunologic, so prior exposure is not required, and heat and moisture worsen it. [2] Blisters may leave brown or purplish marks lasting years. [2]
No studies found for lemon juice as a skin lightener.
